summary: The second list of socket numbers assigned for public functions on the early ARPANET, expanded to include more experimental sockets and new assignments for standard, host-specific and experimental functions. It describes the 40-bit socket structure. It obsoletes RFC 433 and was replaced by RFC 739.

plainLanguage.summary: An updated phone book of the special numbers computers use to find services on the early network, with more entries than before.

subtitle: How network programs find each other using socket numbers

tldr.problem: Network programs needed a standardized way to identify which service they wanted to connect to on a remote host.
tldr.mechanism: Socket numbers were assigned by function: 0-63 for network-wide standard functions, 64-127 for host-specific services, and 128-255 for future or experimental use.
tldr.outcome: The socket system became foundational to early network protocols; servers listened on well-known sockets and clients connected to them via the ICP (Initial Connection Procedure).

today: RFC 503 is Historic and was obsoleted by RFC 739. The socket-number system itself evolved into port numbers in TCP and UDP, which serve the same purpose on the modern internet.

sections.title: Socket Numbers on the ARPANET
sections.content:
RFC 503 is the second published list of socket numbers for the ARPANET. It expands on RFC 433, adding more experimental sockets and updating assignments for host-specific and standard functions.

A socket number is a 40-bit quantity: 8 bits name the host, 24 bits are site-specific (usually zero), and the last 8 bits—called the AEN (Another Eightbit Number)—identify the service. For standard assignments, the host field ranges across all hosts, the 24-bit field is zero, and only the AEN is given.
sections.plainLanguage: A socket number is like a mailing address on the network. First 8 bits: which computer. Next 24 bits: usually just zeros. Last 8 bits: which service you want.

sections.title: Socket Classes
sections.content:
Sockets fall into four ranges. Sockets 0–63 are network-wide standard functions: Telnet (socket 1), File Transfer (socket 3), Remote Job Entry (socket 5), Echo (socket 7), and others. Sockets 64–127 are host-specific, like NETRJS variants at UCLA-CCN on sockets 71, 73, and 75. Sockets 128–223 are reserved for future use. Sockets 224–255 are open for experimental functions.

The RFC lists assignments for each host that offers services, showing which sockets each site uses for Telnet, File Transfer, Echo, CPYNET, and other functions. Some hosts like UCSB offer graphics terminal sockets with custom numbers.
sections.plainLanguage: Socket numbers are sorted into groups: public services (everyone uses these numbers), local variations (each site can add its own), reserved for later, and anything-goes experimental.

sections.title: Assignment and Conflicts
sections.content:
Jon Postel and Nancy Neigus managed socket assignments. The RFC notes that some existing hosts use sockets that conflict with the standard scheme, and the authors hope to resolve these conflicts with minimal disruption. The RFC invites network users to report missing or incorrect assignments.

The RFC was itself replaced by RFC 739, which continued the tradition of periodic socket number lists as the network grew and services evolved.
sections.plainLanguage: A couple of people at the top kept the list of who uses which number. If you found a mistake or added a new service, you'd tell them and they'd update the list.

references.text: Neigus, N. and Postel, J., "Socket Number List", RFC 503, April 1973.
